title: How to Prepare for Early Retirement Health Insurance Costs (COBRA, ACA)
description: Solving the biggest riddle of FIRE: Healthcare before Medicare.
content:
If you retire at 65, you get Medicare. If you retire at 55, you enter the 'Healthcare Danger Zone.' For early retirees, health insurance is often the single largest monthly expense, sometimes exceeding their mortgage. Relying on COBRA is a temporary fix (18 months), not a strategy. The long-term solution involves navigating the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace and managing your income to qualify for subsidies. This guide explains how to bridge the gap without going broke.

Key Takeaways

  • COBRA Sticker Shock: You pay the full premium plus a 2% admin fee. Expect to pay $800-$2,500/month. Use this only as a short-term bridge.
  • The ACA 'Cliff': Subsidies (tax credits) are based on Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI). Keep your income low, and the government pays most of your premium. Earn too much, and you pay full price.
  • Income Management: To get cheap insurance, you need 'Low Income' but 'High Cash Flow.' Use Cash savings and Roth withdrawals (which don't count as income) to fund your life while keeping MAGI low.
  • HSA Strategy: Pay premiums with post-tax dollars if possible, saving the HSA for deductibles and co-pays. Premiums are generally not an allowed HSA expense (unless on COBRA).

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Inflation Reduction Act' extended enhanced ACA subsidies through 2025. This capped premiums at 8.5% of income for many. However, future legislation could change this, making 'Income Control' vital for early retirees.

The Subsidy Game

How to get a $1,500 plan for $100.

The Goal: Low MAGI

The ACA looks at your taxable income. It does NOT look at your net worth. You can have $5 Million in the bank and still qualify for subsidies if your taxable income is low.

Sources of 'Invisible' Cash

  • Cash Savings: Spending $50,000 from a savings account generates $0 taxable income.
  • Roth IRA: Withdrawals of principal (and earnings after 59.5) are tax-free. $0 MAGI.
  • Taxable Brokerage Principal: If you sell $50k of stock, only the gain (e.g., $10k) is income. The $40k basis is return of capital.

The Trap

If you withdraw $80,000 from a Traditional 401(k), your MAGI is $80,000. Your health insurance premiums will skyrocket. Avoid Traditional withdrawals in early retirement.

The Bridge Plan

  1. Build the Cash Tent: 5 years before retiring, save 2-3 years of living expenses in cash. This allows you to live with $0 taxable income for the first few years of retirement, guaranteeing max health subsidies.
  2. Check the Network: Marketplace plans often have narrow networks (HMOs). Check if your preferred doctor accepts 'Exchange Plans' before you quit your job.
  3. Budget for the Max: Assume you will hit your Out-of-Pocket Max ($9k-$18k) every year. If you don't, it's a bonus. If you do, you are prepared.
  4. Geo-Arbitrage: Health insurance costs vary by zip code. Moving to a different county or state can lower your premiums by 30%.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is COBRA worth it?

Only if you have already met your deductible for the year or are in the middle of treatment. Otherwise, ACA plans are usually cheaper.

What if I earn too little?

If you earn below the Federal Poverty Level (~$20k), you are pushed to Medicaid (in expansion states) or get $0 subsidies (in non-expansion states). You must generate enough taxable income (e.g., do a small Roth conversion) to hit the sweet spot.

Can I use HSA for premiums?

Generally No for ACA plans. Yes for COBRA or Medicare premiums. Know the difference to avoid penalties.
